1.pericope_label: How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! she weepeth sore in the night, and her tears are on her cheeks
debates: Who wrote the book
What occasion the book was composed for
Whether the doubled verb means bitter weeping or unceasing weeping
outliers: Clarke records one dissenting opinion, that the five chapters were written by Daniel and his three companions and by Jeconiah, and remarks that none has ever been converted to it
Keil and Delitzsch hold that the doubled verb expresses intensity rather than continuance, so that she weeps bitterly, against Calvin who takes it of a weeping without intermission
Ellicott would join the clauses of the first verse into one sentence, she is become a widow that was great among the nations
themes: A book named from the word it opens with
A city thought exempt from change because God had chosen it
Places of concourse left unfrequented
Tears that do not stop when night comes

3.pericope_label: Judah is gone into captivity because of affliction: the ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts
debates: Whether the going into captivity is forcible deportation or voluntary flight
What the ways of Zion are
Whether the servitude named is what they suffered or what they inflicted
outliers: Calvin holds that interpreters apply the first verse improperly to the captivity, since the prophet speaks first of a voluntary scattering into Moab and Egypt and only afterwards of exile

Calvin guards the lament over the ceasing feasts by noting that the worship of God was not tied to ceremonies, since Daniel prayed in exile and was heard no less than if he had sacrificed in the Temple
Clarke calls the mourning ways a fine prosopopoeia and sets beside it the laments of Moschus for Bion and of Virgil for Daphnis, where woods and rivers are made to weep
themes: Roads overgrown with grass because no one keeps the feast
A head and a tail exchanged as the law had threatened
Fugitives in every country round about
Priests and virgins named together because the feasts have stopped

6.pericope_label: And from the daughter of Zion all her beauty is departed: Jerusalem hath grievously sinned, therefore she is removed
debates: What the word rendered miseries comes from
Whether the days of affliction or the pleasant things are what is remembered
What the mocking at her sabbaths means
outliers: Calvin sets the lament beside the heathen one in Virgil, where the fall of Troy is blamed on a cruel Jupiter, and observes that the unbelieving vomit blasphemies against God while the Prophet adds that God is a righteous avenger
Clarke reports that the old versions read the word for sabbaths as her habitation, her good things and her breach, and defends the sabbath against the mockery of the heathen satirists
Keil and Delitzsch refuse to make the days of affliction a second object of the verb, since a copula would then be needed which one expositor supplies arbitrarily
themes: Princes running like starved deer
Ingratitude as an abyss that absorbs every blessing
A word coined to mean both an enforced sabbath and an empty one
A city shunned as ceremonially unclean

9.pericope_label: Her filthiness is in her skirts, she remembereth not her last end: the adversary hath spread out his hand upon all her pleasant things
debates: Whether the filthiness in the skirts is the sin or the punishment
Whether the pleasant things are the vessels of the sanctuary only
Whether the famine described belongs to the siege or to what followed it
outliers: Calvin holds that interpreters are mistaken who take the filthiness of the skirts for the sins of the people, since the reference is to their punishment, which could not be hidden as shame commonly hides its evils
Keil and Delitzsch refuse to restrict the pleasant things to the treasures of the sanctuary, holding that neither the sense of the word nor the structure of the clauses allows it
Ellicott holds that the prayer closing the verse is spoken not by the prophet but by Zion, anticipating the dramatic personation that begins later in the poem
themes: Uncleanness that cannot be kept out of sight
A warning about the end taken from the song of Moses
A sanctuary called the sanctuary of the people
Jewels handed over for a meal

12.pericope_label: Is it nothing to you, all ye that pass by? behold, and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow
debates: How the first two words of the twelfth verse are to be construed
Whether the bones are the fortified places of the city or the inmost parts of a person
Whether the turning back is a defeat in battle or a failure to escape
outliers: Calvin rejects the reading that makes the bones the fortified places, saying it weakens the meaning, and takes them in their proper sense of the inmost parts, where strength is denoted
Keil and Delitzsch reject the proposal that the prophet says he is not crying to the passers-by, since they could not regard a call addressed to God as applying to them
Henry turns the claim that no sorrow is like this one against the reader, since if all troubles were thrown into a common stock and equally divided each would ask for his own again
themes: A cry addressed to strangers on the road
Fire that goes past skin and flesh into the bone
A net that tightens the more it is struggled against
Suffering met with indifference

14.pericope_label: The yoke of my transgressions is bound by his hand: the Lord hath trodden under foot all my mighty men in the midst of me
debates: Whether the word rendered assembly means a congregation or a fixed time
What the treading under foot means
Whether the yoke or God is the subject of the clause about failing strength
outliers: Ellicott notes that here and in thirteen other places in the book the divine name used is Adonai rather than the more usual Jehovah, as though the covenant name were less appropriate in the lips of one under condemnation

Calvin at first prefers to take the word as the fixed time appointed by God, but grants that to call a fixed time against a person is no suitable expression, so that the received rendering is no doubt right
Keil and Delitzsch take the verb of the fifteenth verse for one meaning to tear away forcibly, and reject the sense that would make the warriors weights raised in a balance
themes: A yoke whose reins are held in the hand that tied it
A festival proclaimed against a city rather than for it
Warriors killed in the middle of their own city
Judgments twisted together like cords

17.pericope_label: Zion spreadeth forth her hands, and there is none to comfort her: the Lord is righteous, for I have rebelled against his commandment
debates: What the spreading of the hands means
Whether the calling to the lovers belongs wholly to the past
Whether anything has dropped from the end of the last verse
outliers: Calvin calls extremely puerile the notion that the clause means Jerusalem had broken bread with her hands, and refuses the rendering that she clapped them as a harsh mode of speaking
Ellicott prefers the suggestive silence of the Hebrew to the words and found not, which two old versions supply at the end of the verse by conjecture
Ellicott observes that with this beginning of conversion the name Jehovah reappears, where the book had been using the other divine name
themes: A pause in the lament where the weeper is choked with tears
Neighbours who are the bitterest foes
Prophetic teaching called the mouth of God
Priests and elders dead of hunger

20.pericope_label: Behold, O Lord, for I am in distress: they are glad that thou hast done it; thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called
debates: What the word rendered troubled means
Whether the day to be brought is the punishment of Judah or of her enemies
Whether the closing words are a wish or a prediction
outliers: Clarke holds that imprecations in the sacred writings are generally declarative of the evils they name, since no prophet of God ever wished desolation on those he was sent to prophesy against
Keil and Delitzsch decline to derive the word for troubled from the root meaning to be red and refer it instead to one meaning to ferment or rise into froth
Ellicott takes the small word before death as giving the emphasis of the undefined, since what makes each home tremble is not death simply but its many shapes
themes: A sufferer turning from strangers to lovers and at last to God
Sorrows unburdened into the bosom of God
Death appearing in sundry shapes
A day proclaimed before it is brought
